vignette:
Kofi's Story

Kofi was thirty-three when the bomb went off at the market in Accra. He had been there for less than five minutes, moving through the vendor stalls near the cloth section where he bought fabric for his tailoring business. The explosion came from somewhere behind him—he never saw it clearly, never understood exactly where. What he remembered was the sound, a rupture that seemed to come from inside his own body, and then the smell of smoke and burning. After that, the sequence fractured. He remembered running, remembered the weight of someone else's arm across his shoulders as he was pulled away, remembered the sirens. But the moments between these fragments were simply gone, erased, as if his mind had stopped recording. He could not recall how he got out of the market or who had helped him. The harder he tried to reconstruct those missing pieces, the more frustrated and afraid he became, certain that if he could only remember, he might understand what he should have done differently.

When Kofi moved to Atlanta three years later, he told himself it was for a fresh start—better opportunities, a chance to build his tailoring business without the weight of that day. But the trauma had traveled with him. The nightmares began within weeks of arriving in America, though they were not quite nightmares. Instead, the memory of the explosion would replay in his mind with mechanical precision, over and over, like a film stuck on a loop. He could feel it happening even in daylight—the blast, the smoke, the confusion—but he experienced it as if watching from outside himself, numb and detached, as if the terror belonged to someone else entirely. This strange dissociation terrified him more than the memory itself. If he could not feel the fear, how could he trust his own judgment about what was real or dangerous? The numbness convinced him that something fundamental had broken inside him. He began to believe he was weak, that a stronger person would have reacted differently in that market, would have protected others, would have been able to remember everything clearly. He was certain now that he could not trust himself to make the right decisions.

These beliefs about his own weakness and untrustworthiness drove him to seek distractions that felt increasingly compulsive. He would spend entire evenings scrolling through his phone, playing games that demanded his full attention, anything to interrupt the replay of the market and the crushing sense that he was fundamentally flawed. When the scrolling and gaming grew stale, he began picking fights with friends and colleagues—small provocations that escalated into arguments about nothing. A customer would comment on a hem, and Kofi would snap at him, manufacturing conflict as if the drama itself could drown out the internal noise. These confrontations left him isolated, but the isolation only deepened his conviction that he belonged nowhere, that even here in America, in his own shop, he was an outsider.

The threat vigilance that had emerged alongside the memory replay now wove itself into everything he did. Every time Kofi entered his tailor shop in the mornings, he would scan for exits—the front door, the back corridor, the window—before he could settle into work. He felt unsafe unless his back was against the wall of his fitting room, where he could see the entire space in front of him. This hypervigilance, born from the fragmentary and replaying memories of the market, reinforced his conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that he was too weak to navigate it. His scanning and wall-positioning became automatic, but they also became evidence to his mind that threat was real, that his fear was justified, that his weakness was proven by his need for these protective positions. The more he needed them, the more he believed he was inadequate.

Months passed in this tightening cycle. Kofi's business suffered as he spent more hours on his phone and less time with clients. His few friendships frayed under the weight of his manufactured arguments. He began making excuses to avoid any plans beyond the immediate day—refusing invitations, canceling appointments, unable to imagine a future in which he might feel safe or competent. The thought of planning anything felt impossible, another confirmation of his weakness and his fundamental unsuitability for normal life. It was only when his sister called from Ghana, worried after weeks of his brief, dismissive messages, that he finally acknowledged something had to change. He was exhausted by the loop, terrified by how much smaller his world had become, and desperate to understand why he could not simply move on. Last month, he made an appointment with a therapist, hoping someone could help him understand what was broken inside him and whether it could ever be repaired.
